h: Gandhi's four pillars of swaraj: a hundred years on, every one is cracked
dek: Ramachandra Guha tests the four conditions for swaraj that Gandhi set out in 1922 against today's India, and the result is unsettling.
body: In 1922 Gandhi said that swaraj (self-rule) would stand on four pillars: the end of untouchability, khadi, Hindu-Muslim unity and non-violence. On Gandhi Jayanti (Gandhi's birth anniversary), historian Ramachandra Guha picks up these same four pillars to see how strong they remain a hundred years later.

Guha does not limit the first pillar to untouchability alone. He reads it as the larger question of caste and gender equality. He accepts that Gandhi called untouchability a sin and brought women forward into public life, but his thinking on women's economic role was conflicted, and a word like 'Harijan' now sounds patronising and insulting.

For Gandhi, khadi was more than cloth. It stood for the dignity of labour and local self-reliance. Guha says that in this age of wealth piling up in a few hands and the ruin of nature, the idea still stands as an alternative.

Gandhi learnt the lesson of Hindu-Muslim unity in South Africa, and he paid for this belief with his life in 1948. On non-violence, he favoured patient collective struggle over lone revolutionary exploits. Guha counts the anti-CAA movement, the farmers' movement, and environmental and student movements in this tradition.

On the other side, he points to critics being jailed under harsh laws, and to divisive rhetoric from the Prime Minister, the Home Minister and several Chief Ministers. His conclusion is that all four pillars have been eaten away, some by the government and some by us citizens. Swaraj has not collapsed, but it is neither strong nor stable.
nazar: Guha's test matters because these four pillars connect directly to the people under the most pressure today: Dalits, Muslims, women and those who work with their hands.
Laying flowers for Gandhi is easy; keeping the conditions of his swaraj is hard. This piece asks for an account of that gap.
sawal: Who has ended up with Gandhi's swaraj today?
ref: Swaraj
For Gandhi, swaraj meant not just freedom from the British but each person's rule over oneself and equality in society. He set out its outline in 'Hind Swaraj' (1909).
Khadi
Hand-spun, hand-woven cloth is called khadi or khaddar. In the freedom struggle it became a symbol of the boycott of foreign cloth and of rural livelihoods.

h: The law on election commissioners kept working while the Supreme Court kept putting off the hearing
dek: A challenge to the law on appointing election commissioners has hung in limbo for two and a half years, and appointments kept being made under that same law.
body: In 2023, in the Anoop Baranwal case, the Supreme Court said that until Parliament made a law, election commissioners would be chosen by a committee of the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and the Chief Justice of India. Within a few months the government brought a new law that put a Union minister picked by the Prime Minister in place of the Chief Justice. In other words, a sure government majority on the committee.

The law was challenged in January 2024 in Jaya Thakur vs Union of India. The writers point out that two and a half years later there has been no proper hearing, let alone a verdict. On 23 September 2026 a two-judge bench split over whether to send the case to a larger bench, and the file went back to the Chief Justice once again, with no date.

Meanwhile the law kept doing its work. Two election commissioners were appointed under it before the 2024 general election, and in February 2025 Gyanesh Kumar became Chief Election Commissioner. Today people on the streets are demanding his resignation.

The writers' real complaint is with the court's internal ways of working. Which case goes to which bench, and when it is heard, is decided by unwritten rules whose key lies with the Chief Justice. Because of this opacity, a constitutional challenge can lie untouched indefinitely.
Their conclusion is that rights mean nothing if courts do not rule on their violation in time, especially when the delay comes from an administrative process whose rules nobody even knows.
nazar: Trust in the Election Commission is the foundation of democracy. When the very method of appointing it is in question and the court stays silent, the biggest loser is the ordinary voter, who has no power except the vote.
Delay in justice is also a decision, and it often goes in favour of the powerful.
sawal: If the court will not decide, who will protect the Constitution?
ref: Master of the roster
The Chief Justice of India's power to decide which case goes before which bench. The Supreme Court confirmed this power in 2018.
Anoop Baranwal judgment
A 2023 Supreme Court judgment that set up a committee of the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and the Chief Justice to select election commissioners, until Parliament made a law.

h: The more the baton swings, the more power loses its standing
dek: Varsha Tiwari argues that the government's decade-long aura of dominance has begun to crack, and its use of force is weakening it further.
body: Delhi writer and translator Varsha Tiwari writes that over the past decade the government's dominance rested on three things: control of the story, management of the media and silencing citizens' voices. Now cracks have begun to show in this building.

In her view the turning point came in July 2026, when young people gathered at Jantar Mantar against the NEET paper leak and challenged the illusion that the government was 'invincible'. Instead of reform, the government chose stubbornness and force.

The writer reminds us that any state's legitimacy rests on three things: it listens to grievances, the law behaves in predictable ways, and the administration is fair. Names being struck off voter lists and the questions raised about the Chief Election Commissioner have broken all three. The police crackdown on protesters on 2 October, Gandhi Jayanti, shows that the more force is used, the more defiance it breeds.

She also draws attention to new leaders, such as AISA president Neha Bora, who went on a 23-day hunger strike and whose language is direct and clear. Tiwari says fascism fills language with hollow slogans so that the line between truth and lies blurs, and journalists, young satirists and Gen Z leaders are standing up against exactly this.
Her conclusion is that this mobilisation over the honesty of elections is a real crisis of legitimacy for the government.
nazar: This piece is a reminder that in a democracy, power draws its strength not from the stick but from people's trust. When young people, students and ordinary voters start asking questions together, answering them is the only way forward.
sawal: Can power that rests on fear ever earn trust?
ref: AISA
All India Students' Association, a left student organisation active in many universities across the country.
NEET
The national entrance exam for admission to medical colleges. Students across the country have protested against allegations that its paper was leaked.

h: When does crowd control become excess? There are rules, but no accountability
dek: Aman Khanna shows that rules exist for the use of force on protesters, yet police brutality keeps coming back.
body: On 20 July at Jantar Mantar, police allegedly used nail-studded lathis (batons), rubber bullets and pellet guns on protesters from the Cockroach Janata Party. The Supreme Court had to set up an inquiry committee. Aman Khanna uses this incident to ask where exactly the police's limits lie.

There is no shortage of rules on paper. The Home Ministry's 1985 guidelines say force should be only as much as is absolutely necessary, in line with United Nations principles. Delhi Police Standing Order 72 also speaks of maximum restraint and minimum injury. Article 19(1)(b) of the Constitution gives the right to assemble peacefully, and Article 19(3) leaves room to restrict it in the name of public order. The police work between these two.

Yet the same story was repeated at Aarey Colony (2019), in the Jallikattu movement (2017) and in the wage protests in Noida (2024). Khanna points out that several essential things are missing from the guidelines: the ratio of police to the size of the crowd, a test for judging the threat, and exit routes for the crowd. By contrast, a model from Stanford Law School requires an officer to weigh several factors before declaring a situation a riot.

The real disease is accountability. In a 2025 survey, 70 percent of police personnel agreed that force can be used without punishment. The writer concludes that until there is enforceable accountability, the rules on paper will stay meaningless.
nazar: Workers, farmers, students and people on the margins face the police lathi the most, because the street is all they have left to make themselves heard. The right to protest is real only when those who crush it can be held to account.
sawal: When there is no fear of punishment, who are the rules for?
ref: Article 19(1)(b)
The constitutional provision that gives every citizen the fundamental right to assemble peacefully and without arms.
Standing order
Written rules for the police's internal working that set out what officers should and should not do in a given situation.

h: A name on the UNESCO list, but no promise of protection on the ground
dek: India's UNESCO tentative list now has 78 sites, but Dipanjana Saha asks what this changes on the ground, especially for the indigenous people of Nicobar.
body: On 29 September India added five new sites to its UNESCO World Heritage tentative list, including the Bagh cave paintings and the colonial penal settlement in the Andamans. The list now stands at 78. Dipanjana Saha reminds us that this is only a planning stage. It is no legal protection, and no curb on development.

As an example she describes what happened to Narcondam Island. This small volcanic island is home to the rare Narcondam hornbill and came onto the list in 2014. That same year the Environment Ministry approved a radar station there. The plan was later halted, but not because of the list. It stopped because of public protest and scrutiny.

The piece's gravest concern is for the native people of Nicobar. The new entry, 'Nicobarese cultural continuity', covers seven islands of central Nicobar. UNESCO's rules require the free, prior and informed consent of indigenous people. The writer asks whether this consultation took place, and whether its record will be made public.
She links this to the large Great Nicobar project, where the tribal council withdrew its consent in 2022 and petitions on the consent process are pending in the Calcutta High Court.

Saha suggests three tests for every such listing: the heritage, forest and wildlife departments should protect the site together; the people who live there should be treated as decision-makers, not just 'stakeholders'; and the results on upkeep, the environment and benefits to communities should be made public.
nazar: A heritage badge is hollow until the Adivasi (indigenous) communities who live that heritage are asked. In Nicobar the question is not just about putting culture on display; it is about the right to land and to life.
sawal: How can anyone's heritage be saved without asking them?
ref: Tentative list
UNESCO's Tentative List, where a country places sites it wants to nominate for World Heritage status later on.
Free, prior and informed consent
The right of indigenous people that any project on their land goes ahead only with their approval, given in advance, with full information and without pressure.

h: Don't turn water into a weapon: Dawn's appeal on the Indus Waters Treaty
dek: A Dawn editorial calls India's suspension of the Indus Waters Treaty a dangerous precedent and appeals to both countries to return to the path of talks.
body: An editorial in the Pakistani newspaper Dawn counts the Indus Waters Treaty, along with Kashmir, among the two biggest disputes between the two countries. After the Pahalgam attack in 2025, India unilaterally suspended the treaty and said it would not be restored until Pakistan acted against cross-border terrorism.

The paper sees this as morally wrong and a dangerous international precedent, in which an upstream country uses river water as a weapon. The editorial mentions Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's statement that diverting water would be an act of war, and also Information Minister Attaullah Tarar's warning that India's move threatens water-sharing arrangements around the world.

One key fact is that in August 2026 the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague said the treaty cannot be suspended unilaterally, and India rejected that ruling. Dawn argues that India speaks of a rules-based order on world platforms but is ignoring international law in this case.

The editorial stresses that the Indus and its tributaries are Pakistan's lifeline, so there can be no compromise on the right to water. Keeping the dispute hanging could push the region towards conflict.
Finally the paper appeals to the sensible sections of India to restore the treaty and open the way for diplomacy.
nazar: This is Pakistan's view, but part of it is worth thinking about for India too. River water is the life of farmers and the poor on both sides. They are the first to pay the price of war and stubbornness, on this side of the border and on that.
For peace in South Asia, water should be a bridge for dialogue, not a weapon.
sawal: Should rivers too be dragged into hostility across the border?
ref: Indus Waters Treaty

A treaty signed between India and Pakistan in 1960 with the World Bank as mediator. The eastern rivers Ravi, Beas and Sutlej went to India, and the western rivers Indus, Jhelum and Chenab to Pakistan.
Permanent Court of Arbitration
An intergovernmental body based in The Hague that arbitrates disputes between countries.

h: Denying caste, ignoring women: blindness on both sides
dek: Dr Saraswati Suna shows how we put on selective lenses when we read literature, love and society, lenses that hide some injustices.
body: The writer begins by noting that literature is both a mirror of society and a force that shapes it. But readers read a work through lenses of their own choosing, so some inequalities come into view and others drop out of sight.

Her main example is the response to Odia poet Basudev Sunani's poem 'Dholia' (the drummer). The poem is about the love and life of a man from the Dhulia community, a Dalit caste of drummers. Some readers saw only romance in it, while others saw that caste is present everywhere in the poem, even though it is never named.

From this she shows that caste shapes love and relationships even when it seems absent. Then she speaks of a double blindness. Many upper-caste feminists deny caste in the name of 'progress', and some Dalit Ambedkarite men push aside the question of gender in the name of 'unity'. Both protect their own privilege.

Drawing on Ambedkar's essay 'Castes in India', she explains that patriarchy keeps caste alive precisely by controlling women's sexuality and enforcing marriage within the caste. She links this to Kimberlé Crenshaw's idea of intersectionality.
Her conclusion: Dalit women face caste oppression and patriarchy at the same time, both in the mainstream and inside anti-caste circles. Refusing to see caste or gender does not make them disappear.
nazar: The question of Dalit women does not fit into the frame of any one movement. Any fight for social justice is incomplete until it takes up the questions of caste and of women together.
sawal: Do we see only the injustice that hurts us?
ref: Endogamy
The practice of marrying only within one's own caste or group. Ambedkar called it the root of the caste system.
Intersectionality
An idea from American legal scholar Kimberlé Crenshaw: identities such as caste, race and gender combine to create distinct and deeper forms of discrimination.

h: Delhi Police can do better, and once it did
dek: Rohit Kumar, who once taught police trainees, sets Delhi Police's brutality at the Gandhi Jayanti protests against his own memories of the past.
body: Rohit Kumar says Delhi Police's action against the protests held over the Gandhi Jayanti weekend, demanding the removal of the Chief Election Commissioner, will be remembered for its scale and cruelty. AISA president Neha Bora was picked up in an unmarked vehicle, and a police station refused to register a case against an officer accused of sexually harassing a woman journalist.
Against this the writer sets his memories from around 1999, when he was training about twelve hundred probationary sub-inspectors in communication at the Police Training College in Delhi.

In one exercise he asked the recruits to describe a time they had helped an ordinary citizen. Kiran Bedi, then Joint Commissioner, collected these stories in a booklet titled 'When I Reached Out' and made it part of the syllabus. For the writer this is proof that the humanity inside the uniform can be awakened.
He draws on Hannah Arendt's idea of the 'banality of evil': great atrocities are often carried out by ordinary people following orders, without thinking about what they are doing.

His conclusion is that Delhi Police may be at its lowest point today, but reform is possible. An institution's values come from its leadership, and the leadership of Delhi Police lies with the Home Ministry.
nazar: The mistreatment of women journalists at the protests, and the refusal even to register a complaint, show that when the police themselves rise above the law, women and the weaker sections are the most unsafe.
The piece's hope matters too: police culture is not a law of nature. It can be changed.
sawal: When will the constable who follows orders learn to ask questions?
ref: Banality of evil
Philosopher Hannah Arendt's idea, put forward while writing on the trial of Nazi officer Eichmann: terrible crimes are often committed by ordinary people obeying orders without thinking.
FIR
First Information Report. Once it is registered, the police begin investigating a cognisable offence.

h: The white coat is either safe everywhere, or nowhere
dek: MSF's international president urges the World Medical Association to make the release of Palestinian doctors held in Israeli detention its first priority.
body: Javid Abdelmoneim, international president of Doctors Without Borders (MSF), writes this piece on the occasion of the World Medical Association's general assembly in Rotterdam. His demand is clear: the question of detained Palestinian health workers should be at the top of the agenda.

According to him, more than 1,700 medical workers have been killed in the Gaza war. Hundreds were detained without any charge, and more than 80 are still in custody. He names three: paediatrician and former hospital director Hussam Abu Safiya, held for more than 22 months; 71-year-old family doctor Mazin al-Rantisi; and MSF orthopaedic surgeon Mohammed Obeid, in detention for more than 600 days.

The writer cites World Health Organization figures showing about a thousand attacks on health facilities in Gaza, with nearly 90 percent of its health infrastructure destroyed. In the West Bank too, more than a thousand attacks on health services have been recorded since October 2023, and ambulances are stopped at checkpoints.
He argues that protecting doctors and nurses is a universal moral principle, one that cannot change according to geography or politics.

The World Medical Association has passed resolutions on such protection before. The writer says it is now time to get them enforced, by putting pressure on governments and national medical associations. This assembly is a test of whether medical neutrality still means anything when there is a price to pay.
nazar: This is a question for India's doctors and their associations too. How can a profession that begins with an oath to save human life stay silent about the imprisonment of its own colleagues?
sawal: Has giving medical care now become a crime as well?
ref: World Medical Association
A federation of national medical associations from around the world that sets ethical standards for doctors, such as the Declaration of Geneva.
MSF
Médecins Sans Frontières, or Doctors Without Borders, an international medical organisation that works in areas hit by war and disaster.

h: The dream of gas from dung: the portal is built, now the ground needs the structure
dek: The new GOBARdhan scheme brings the biogas sector under one umbrella, but the writers say the real test will come in the states and districts.
body: On 1 October the central government relaunched the GOBARdhan scheme in a new form. The aim is to bring the scattered compressed biogas (CBG) sector into one framework, so that land, raw material, clearances, money and gas sales do not wander between separate offices.

The writers give the background: in 2024-25 India imported about 14.9 billion dollars' worth of natural gas. Gas made from crop residue, cattle dung and organic waste can reduce this dependence and turn farm waste into something useful.

Under the scheme, every plant must register on a digital portal and will be monitored in real time. Capital support goes up to Rs 1.25 crore per tonne of daily capacity, but the final half of the money comes only when the plant starts using 75 percent of its capacity. A fund of Rs 500 crore will reward districts that do well on clearances, identifying raw material and using organic manure. Gas purchases will be covered by three-way agreements with penalties.

But according to the writers, the real hurdles remain: a reliable supply of raw material, a market for the organic manure left over after the gas is made, and pipeline infrastructure. None of this will happen without the states taking the lead.

Their conclusion is that the question is whether states and districts can build a system around each plant that links farmers, collection centres and the gas market. Only then will the portal move off paper and onto the ground.
nazar: If dung and parali (crop stubble) become a source of income for farmers, that is good news both for the village economy and for clean air. But the fear is that the gains get confined to big companies, and small livestock keepers are left as mere suppliers of raw material.
sawal: Will the money from dung reach the livestock keeper's pocket?
ref: Compressed biogas
Fuel made by cleaning and compressing gas produced from organic waste. It can be used in place of CNG.
Digestate
The nutrient-rich slurry left over after biogas is produced. It can be put on fields as organic manure.

h: 24 million need help, and not even one counsellor for every 500,000 people
dek: A Dawn editorial welcomes Pakistan's new mental health policy but says it will stay on paper unless attitudes change.
body: According to an estimate by Pakistan's federal health minister, about 24 million people in the country need mental health support. Yet there is not even one therapist for every 500,000 people. Dawn's editorial begins with this gap.

The government has just launched a national mental health policy that aims to take treatment out of big hospitals and into primary health centres and communities. It provides a national framework and gives the provinces freedom to adapt it to their needs. The focus is on early detection, treatment and rehabilitation.

The editorial reminds us that untreated illness costs both health and the economy. In times of social stress, depression and anxiety rise, and the climate crisis and digital life are wearing down people's resilience. Shame and stigma make people hesitate to seek help. Depression is diagnosed twice as often in women as in men, and mental illness keeps children away from school and adults away from work.

According to the paper, the policy will succeed only if society's attitude changes, the number of counsellors grows and general doctors are trained to recognise symptoms. It warns against over-reliance on medicines and says treatment must be affordable.
The conclusion: only open and continuous conversation about mental health breaks old myths, and the cost of sitting idle is very heavy.
nazar: India's picture is not very different. Here too mental health care is confined to cities and the well-off, while village women, workers and unemployed young people carry their burden in silence. This debate next door is a mirror for us as well.
sawal: When will we speak openly about pain of the mind?
ref: Community-based care
An approach to mental health care in which treatment is given through local clinics and health workers instead of large psychiatric hospitals.

h: Young enough to protest, not to run for office
dek: In West Africa the legal age barrier has gone, but a wall of money still keeps young people away from power.
body: About 70 percent of West Africa's population is young. Adesewa Olofinko writes that the legal hurdles on the age for contesting elections have largely gone, but walls of money and structure still keep young people out.

Nigeria is an example. In 2018 the 'Not Too Young To Run' campaign won a constitutional amendment lowering the age for candidacy. Eight years later, the nomination form for the presidency costs up to 100 million naira, and in one state the form for a local council chairman's election cost 30 million naira, more than four years' salary for that post. The new election law of February 2026 doubled the spending limit, which helps rich candidates.

The piece records voices from the West Africa Youth Democracy Summit held in Dakar in September, attended by delegates from 12 countries. A Ghanaian MP said young people are made the face on the poster but are not given real power. One activist pointed to the contradiction that young people can vote and take to the streets, but are called 'inexperienced' when it comes to office.
In the background, Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger leaving ECOWAS has cut millions of young people off from this regional platform. The summit led to the creation of a youth observer network.
The writer concludes that African youth have shown they can get election rules changed. Bringing down the wall of money is a far harder fight.
nazar: This story is not unfamiliar in India either. Here too elections have become so expensive that a young person from a worker's, farmer's, Dalit or Adivasi family can build a movement but cannot bear the burden of the ticket and the campaign costs.
sawal: When elections are bought, through which door do young people get in?
ref: ECOWAS
The Economic Community of West African States, a regional body of 15 countries, from which three military-ruled countries broke away in 2025.
Alliance of Sahel States
A union formed by the military governments of Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger after they left ECOWAS.

h: Point the finger at one man, and the whole system walks free
dek: Yoav Litvin argues that Israel's election question, whether Netanyahu knew in advance or not, is a way of escaping a real reckoning.
body: Psychologist and writer Yoav Litvin writes that Israel's election campaign is stuck on one question: did Prime Minister Netanyahu know about the 7 October attack in advance? Litvin sees this not as accountability but as a psychological defence: put all the blame on one man, and the rest of the system gets away clean.

In his view, many questions are missing from the Israeli debate: military operations that put hostages' lives at risk, rejected ceasefire proposals, and the International Criminal Court's arrest warrants against Netanyahu and former defence minister Gallant.

The writer's main claim is that the issue is not just denial or misinformation, but the complicity of a large part of society. He mentions the thousands of Palestinians killed in Gaza, large-scale arbitrary arrests, the targeting of journalists and doctors, and the destruction of hospitals and cultural heritage, along with the operations in Lebanon, Syria and Yemen.
Litvin places this within the framework of settler colonialism, where portraying others as less than human becomes a way of keeping public consent.

His conclusion is that this election is not a reckoning but one more way of avoiding it. If only Netanyahu is replaced without questioning the basic structure of domination, that structure may grow even deeper.
nazar: This piece is a warning for any democracy: when the whole debate shrinks to one leader, the policies and thinking whose price the weakest people pay slip away untouched.
sawal: Does changing the face change the intent?
ref: International Criminal Court
A court based in The Hague that tries cases of war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide. In November 2024 it issued warrants against Netanyahu and Gallant.

h: Children online, protection offline
dek: A Dawn editorial says children's safety on the internet will come not from bans but from a shared effort by the law, companies, schools and parents.
body: Dawn's editorial points to a growing gap: Pakistani children are spending more time on the internet than ever before, but there is very little in place to protect them there.

According to a Kaspersky survey, children's favourite apps are YouTube, Instagram and WhatsApp. Multiplayer games and chat platforms bring them into contact with strangers, where there is a risk of grooming, fraud and blackmail. Deepfakes made with generative AI have now become a new tool for harassing children.

The biggest problem is regulation. The Pakistan Telecommunication Authority told the Islamabad High Court that it has no legal power either to make age checks compulsory or to bar those under 16 from social media. It says that because of encryption, blocking specific content is not possible without shutting down the whole platform. Changes to the cybercrime law in 2025 created a new authority, which tangled responsibility even further.

The paper sees a total ban as an easy but wrong path. It advises that companies make children's accounts safe and offer an easy way to complain, schools teach children to recognise digital dangers, and parents talk openly with their children.
The conclusion: protecting children needs clear laws, responsible tech companies, better digital education and aware families, all together.
nazar: In India too, crores (tens of millions) of children are online thanks to cheap data, especially in small towns and villages, where understanding of digital dangers is lowest. This approach of shared responsibility instead of bans is useful for us as well.
sawal: The child has a phone in hand, but who is by their side?
ref: PECA
Pakistan's Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act, 2016, amended in 2025 to create a new regulatory authority for social media.
Grooming
The process of building a relationship with a child, winning their trust, with the intention of exploiting them.

h: Farmers' real anger, inflated online and then hijacked
dek: A data-driven analysis of a farmers' protest in Romania shows how genuine grievances get swept away in a wave of disinformation.
body: On 15 September hundreds of farmers gathered in Bucharest, Romania's capital, against a European Union ban on livestock exports. They wanted compensation for animals that had been culled and for losses from drought. The protest began peacefully but later turned violent: 24 people needed medical care and 47 were taken to police stations.

Researchers from the civic group Funky Citizens went through 1,186 Facebook posts and 100 TikTok videos. They found that on the evening before the protest, within just fifteen minutes, dozens of pages posted almost identical claims that about two lakh (200,000) farmers would come. In reality around three thousand turned up. Two clusters of roughly fifty accounts each were behind most of the engagement across the whole network.

Four stories emerged online: the farmers' economic demands, police harshness, the presence of George Simion, leader of the far-right party AUR, and the structural problems of farming. On Telegram, two channels already identified as pro-Kremlin changed their tune three times within a few hours that same day, from listing demands, to warning of a conspiracy, to attacking the media.

The writers conclude that a legitimate rural grievance was first amplified and exaggerated, then folded into anti-government, anti-EU and pro-Kremlin narratives. They say clearly that who was behind this, and why, has not yet been proven.
nazar: India's farmers' movement has also seen how genuine demands on social media are either smeared or tied to some other agenda. This study shows how important it is to hear the farmer's voice in the farmer's own words.
sawal: Whose voice gets mixed into the farmer's voice?
ref: AUR
Alliance for the Union of Romanians, a far-right nationalist party in Romania.
Coordinated inauthentic behaviour
Networks of accounts that work together to spread content artificially, so it looks more popular than it really is.

h: When Bangla poetry took to the streets
dek: Baby Shaw's essay tells the story of Bangla poetry's changing temper in the era of the Naxalbari movement.
body: In this instalment of the column 'C/O Bengal' on Hindwi Bela, Baby Shaw begins in Kolkata in 1971, when poet, translator and editor of the magazine 'Parichay' Saroj Dutta disappeared after his arrest. To this day there is no official record of how he died. Saroj Dutta joined the communist movement in 1949 and was among the founders of the CPI (ML) in 1969.

The essay's central argument is that Naxalbari turned Bangla poetry away from private introspection and towards collective consciousness. Plain, restless language replaced ornament, and the subjects became labour, hunger and the violence of the state.

The writer remembers many poets of that time, including names like Birendra Chattopadhyay and Shankha Ghosh. She describes how poems travelled through leaflets, wall writing and underground publications, and how poetry and struggle were no longer separate from each other.
nazar: This essay reminds us that poetry lives not only in books but also on walls and in leaflets, and that bearing witness against state violence is an old duty of literature.
sawal: Can today's poetry take to the streets again?
ref: Naxalbari movement
A peasant uprising in 1967 in the Naxalbari area of Darjeeling district, led by Charu Majumdar and Kanu Sanyal, which led to the formation of the CPI (ML) in 1969.

h: The strange and deep 'tail' of Riyaz Latif's nazms
dek: Reading Urdu poet Riyaz Latif's collection 'Nazm ki Poonchh', Nishant Kaushik shows how the book challenges the very structure of the nazm.
body: In his column 'Jagah-Jagah 2.0' (Here and There 2.0), Nishant Kaushik writes about Urdu poet and translator Riyaz Latif's collection 'Nazm ki Poonchh' (The Tail of the Nazm). His main point is that the 'tail' here works in two ways: on one side it is a funny, absurd device, and on the other a philosophical figure with a life of its own.

According to the reviewer, these nazms (poems) wrestle with existence, non-existence, emptiness and death, but without striking an existentialist pose. They have a kind of impudence that erases the line between the sacred and the bodily.

Kaushik puts special stress on the range of Latif's learning. His study of architecture and art history has given room in these poems to Córdoba and the Alhambra, Egyptian hieroglyphs, cuneiform script, the Shahnameh tradition and South Asian cultural memory, all of it. The essay presents the book as a work that breaks the traditional shape of the nazm.
nazar: Such a serious reading of new Urdu poetry reaching Hindi readers strengthens the shared heritage of the Hindustani language.
sawal: Can absurdity also be a way of saying something deep?
ref: Nazm
A form of Urdu poetry in which the whole poem moves as one unit on a single theme, whereas each couplet of a ghazal is complete in itself. Iqbal, Faiz and Miraji are its great names.

h: Who will be the face of Hindi poetry abroad?
dek: Pankaj Prakhar's sharp essay asks whether Hindi poetry's representation on international platforms is decided by work or by publicity.
body: In the column 'Sarsari' (In Passing), Pankaj Prakhar uses an international poetry and literature festival in China to raise the question of how Hindi poetry is represented. He alleges that people with weak literary standing now reach foreign platforms through self-promotion and social media rather than the quality of their writing, and that this lowers the standing of Hindi literature in the world.
Against this he recalls history, when scholar-monks such as Kashyapa Matanga, Dharmaraksha, Kumarajiva and Paramartha carried Indian thought to China through serious study and translation.

The writer also mentions a conversation with a Chinese friend, who compared today's Hindi poetry scene to a pop music market where real voices are drowned out and average faces shine. The essay ends with a reference to a poem by Polish poet Tadeusz Różewicz, in Asad Zaidi's translation, which hints that the problem of fake poets has always been with us.
nazar: This debate is not just about trips abroad; it is about honesty in literature. When platforms go to those who promote themselves, the real voices from small towns and the margins are the first to be left behind.
sawal: Will a poet be known by the poem, or by the reel?
ref: Kumarajiva
(344-413 CE) A Buddhist monk-scholar from Kucha who lived in China and translated Sanskrit Buddhist texts into Chinese, including the 'Lotus Sutra' and the 'Diamond Sutra'.

h: A letter to Aristotle: will you change your mind about women?
dek: Ayushman's satirical letter draws Aristotle's attention to the policing of women and the double standards in today's India.
body: This is the seventh in a series of satirical letters addressed to Aristotle, inspired by the tradition of Harishankar Parsai. This time the subject is misogyny and the policing of women in today's India.

The writer lays out a long list of contradictions: young girls worshipped during Navratri (a nine-night festival of the goddess) and denied basic freedom the rest of the year; girls locked into hostels while being taught constitutional equality; 'boys will be boys, they make mistakes' after a rape, and murder in the name of honour for a relationship of one's own choosing. He also hits at the hollowness of the 'Beti Bachao' (Save the Daughter) slogan, and at parties that fight each other but unite on the question of women.

The letter also praises the courage of women who have taken to the streets and their fresh new slogans. Aristotle believed a woman was an incomplete man. The writer asks him whether he will rethink his view, and invites him to meet the strong women of India who are fighting for equality.
nazar: Satire is sharpest where hypocrisy runs deepest. Through laughter, this letter raises the question of women's freedom with just as much seriousness.
sawal: Between worship and policing, what has a woman really been given?
ref: Harishankar Parsai
(1924-1995) One of Hindi's greatest satirists. He won the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1982 for 'Viklang Shraddha ka Daur' (The Age of Crippled Faith).

h: Calvino's invisible cities: names, memory and forgotten faces
dek: The eleventh instalment of Suman Shekhar's serialised translation brings three new cities and a conversation between Marco Polo and Kublai Khan.
body: Sammukh is publishing a Hindi translation of Italo Calvino's famous book 'Invisible Cities' in instalments. In the book, Marco Polo tells Kublai Khan about cities that perhaps exist nowhere.

Three cities appear in this instalment. One is a city whose picture in the mind falls apart the moment you arrive, replaced by straight lanes, scattered houses and dusty air; here the question is the gap between a name and the real place. The second is a city where the narrator keeps seeing the faces of the dead among the living, as if the past were taking over the present. In the third, beneath the chaos of its lanes, the city's true map lies hidden in a carpet.
At the end, a conversation between Marco and Kublai raises the question of whether travel is really a journey within memory. To read the translation, go to the original page.
nazar: Books of world literature like this arriving in easy Hindi widen the Hindi reader's world. It is also a mirror for our own fast-changing cities.
sawal: Do our cities live in our memories, or on maps?
ref: Italo Calvino
(1923-1985) Italian writer known for his experimental and imaginative prose. 'Invisible Cities' was published in 1972.

h: Yvon Le Men, poet of Brittany: the sea, graves and fishermen
dek: Ten poems by French poet Yvon Le Men in Ajit Dash's translation, speaking of what lies between vanishing and surviving.
by: Yvon Le Men (translated by Ajit Dash)
body: Sammukh has published ten poems by Yvon Le Men, a poet from the Brittany region of France, in Ajit Dash's Hindi translation, with a short introduction. The introduction says Le Men was born in Tréguier in 1953, that writing has been his only profession since his first book in 1974, that more than sixty poetry collections have been published, and that he received the Goncourt Prize for Poetry in 2019.

Death and memory are at the centre of the poems: graves, stones, things worn down by time. In his work the sea, waves, mountains, leaves and old farmhouses become a way of thinking about what passes away and what remains.

Some poems show the chain of fisherman, fish and hunger, and look at the poverty of beggars and fishermen with compassion and dignity. The style is extremely spare; the last poem is just four lines and four words. Read the poems on the original page.
nazar: These poems about fishermen on a distant seashore do not feel far from the lives of fishermen on our own coasts. Good translation builds exactly this bond.
sawal: Of what passes away, what remains?
ref: Goncourt Prize for Poetry
The poetry award of France's Académie Goncourt, given since 1985 for a poet's whole body of work.
